source: Scanned from live OMV 8 installation: /usr/share/openmediavault/workbench/ and /usr/share/openmediavault/engined/rpc/

entries.title: OMV 8 Web UI Top-Level Navigation
entries.content: OpenMediaVault 8 web interface top-level navigation sections (all require admin role except Dashboard): Dashboard (/dashboard, position 10, icon: apps) - summary widgets showing system status. System (/system, position 20, icon: laptop) - system-wide settings. Network (/network, position 30, icon: network) - networking configuration. Storage (/storage, position 40, icon: nas) - disk and filesystem management. Services (/services, position 50, icon: share) - file sharing services. Users (/usermgmt, position 60, icon: users) - user and group accounts. Diagnostics (/diagnostics, position 70, icon: heartPulse) - system health and logs. The positions determine menu order. All sections except Dashboard require the admin role to access.

entries.title: Storage Section: All Pages and URLs
entries.content: Storage section (/storage) sub-pages from navigation.d files: 1) Disks (/storage/disks, position 10) - list physical drives, configure hdparm, wipe disks, rescan SCSI. 2) S.M.A.R.T. (/storage/smart, position 20) - disk health monitoring with sub-pages: Settings (/storage/smart/settings), Devices (/storage/smart/devices, enable per-disk monitoring), Scheduled Tasks (/storage/smart/tasks). 3) Multiple Device (/storage/md, position 30) - software RAID via mdadm with routes for: create, grow, recover, remove, details. 4) File Systems (/storage/filesystems, position 40) - filesystem creation (ext4, xfs, btrfs, jfs, f2fs), mounting, growing; routes for each fs type: ext4, xfs, btrfs, f2fs, jfs. 5) Bcache (/storage/bcache, position 15) - SSD block-layer cache with sub-pages for Cache devices and Backing devices. 6) Shared Folders (/storage/shared-folders, position 90) - define named folder paths on mounted filesystems for use by services.

entries.title: Services Section: All Pages and URLs
entries.content: Services section (/services) sub-pages: 1) SMB/CIFS (/services/smb) - Windows file sharing, sub-pages: Settings (/services/smb/settings); Shares (/services/smb/shares). 2) NFS (/services/nfs) - Linux/Unix file sharing, sub-pages: Settings (/services/nfs/settings); Shares (/services/nfs/shares). 3) SSH (/services/ssh) - secure shell access, enable/disable, port, auth options. 4) Rsync (/services/rsync) - sync jobs and daemon, sub-pages: Server Settings, Modules (/services/rsync/server/modules), Tasks. 5) WOL (/services/wol) - Wake-on-LAN packet sender to specific MAC addresses. 6) Locate (/services/locate) - updatedb/locate file indexing database. 7) PWM Fan (/services/pwmfan) - pulse-width modulation fan speed control.

entries.title: System Section: All Pages and URLs
entries.content: System section (/system) sub-pages: 1) Workbench (/system/workbench) - web UI settings: HTTP/HTTPS port, session timeout, SSL certificate selection. 2) Date & Time (/system/date-time) - NTP server configuration, timezone selection. 3) Notification (/system/notification) - email alerts setup: Settings (SMTP config), Events (which events trigger emails). 4) Power Management (/system/powermgmt) - scheduled standby/shutdown/reboot: Settings, Scheduled Tasks. 5) Monitoring (/system/monitoring) - collectd/RRD performance graph settings. 6) Scheduled Tasks (/system/cron) - cron job management. 7) Update Management (/system/updatemgmt) - system updates: Updates list, Settings. 8) Plugins (/system/plugins) - install/remove OMV plugins. 9) Certificates (/system/certificate) - SSL (/system/certificate/ssl) and SSH (/system/certificate/ssh) key management. 10) omv-extras (/system/omvextras) - extra package repositories.

entries.title: Network Section: All Pages and URLs
entries.content: Network section (/network) sub-pages: 1) General (/network/general) - hostname, domain name, DNS servers, IPv4/IPv6 forwarding. 2) Interfaces (/network/interfaces) - configure all network interfaces. Supports: Ethernet (physical NICs), Bond (link aggregation), VLAN (802.1Q), Wireless (WiFi with WPA), Bridge (for VMs). Each interface configurable for DHCP or static IP, MTU, wake-on-LAN. 3) Proxy (/network/proxy) - HTTP/HTTPS proxy configuration for package downloads and updates. 4) Firewall (/network/firewall) - iptables/ip6tables rules management. Sub-page: Rules (/network/firewall/rules) for creating allow/deny rules by protocol, port, source/destination.

entries.title: Diagnostics Section: All Pages and URLs
entries.content: Diagnostics section (/diagnostics) sub-pages: 1) System Information (/diagnostics/system-information) - hardware summary: CPU model, RAM, uptime, kernel version, OMV version, OS version. 2) System Logs (/diagnostics/system-logs) - log file browser: syslog, auth.log, daemon.log, kern.log; Remote (syslog remote server config). 3) Processes (/diagnostics/processes) - real-time process list similar to top. 4) Performance Statistics (/diagnostics/performance-statistics) - RRD/collectd graphs: CPU, Memory, Load, Uptime, Network Interfaces, Disk Usage. 5) Services (/diagnostics/services) - service running status overview for SMB, NFS, SSH. 6) Report (/diagnostics/report) - download full diagnostic report including hardware, network, storage info.

entries.title: Users Section: All Pages and URLs
entries.content: Users section (/usermgmt) sub-pages: 1) Settings (/usermgmt/settings) - default shell for new users, default group assignment. 2) Users (/usermgmt/users) - create, edit, delete user accounts. Fields: username, password, shell, groups membership, email, SSH public keys, comment. 3) Groups (/usermgmt/groups) - create/edit/delete groups, manage group members. Users and groups are real Linux system accounts in /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, /etc/group. The 'admin' account is the OMV web UI administrator only and cannot be used as a shared folder privilege target. Default NAS group is 'users' - shared folder access typically requires membership.

entries.title: Disk Management in OMV (Storage > Disks)
entries.content: The Disks page (Storage > Disks, /storage/disks) lists all physical block devices detected. Information shown per disk: device name (/dev/sdX or by-id path), model, size, vendor, serial number, WWN, temperature (from SMART if enabled), power mode (active/standby). Per-disk configuration (hdparm): spin-down time (in units of 5 seconds, 0=disabled), APM level (1-254, lower=more aggressive power saving), AAM (Automatic Acoustic Management). Wipe disk operation: Quick wipe uses sgdisk --zap-all plus dd to zero first 10MiB and last 10MiB. Secure wipe uses shred -v -n 1. Both destroy all partition tables and data. The OS root disk is shown as read-only and cannot be wiped. Rescan SCSI Bus: writes '- - -' to all /sys/class/scsi_host/host*/scan entries and '1' to /sys/class/scsi_device/*/device/rescan. RPC: DiskMgmt (enumerateDevices, getList, getListBg, getHdParm, setHdParm, wipe, rescan).

entries.title: S.M.A.R.T. Monitoring in OMV
entries.content: S.M.A.R.T. is at Storage > S.M.A.R.T. (/storage/smart). Settings: enable/disable smartd daemon, temperature thresholds for info/warning/critical, polling interval (minutes). Devices: enable per-disk monitoring, device type override (auto, ata, scsi, sat). Scheduled Tasks: configure short/long self-tests per drive on a schedule. CLI: smartctl -a /dev/sdX (all info), smartctl -l selftest /dev/sdX (self-test log), smartctl -H /dev/sdX (health summary). Key SMART attributes: Attr 5 (Reallocated Sectors Count), Attr 9 (Power On Hours), Attr 187 (Reported Uncorrectable Errors), Attr 197 (Current Pending Sector Count), Attr 198 (Offline Uncorrectable). Any non-zero value for attrs 5, 187, 197, 198 is a warning sign. Self-test types: Short (typically 2 min), Long (hours depending on disk size). RPC: Smart (enumerateDevices, enumerateMonitoredDevices, getList, getSettings, setSettings, getDeviceSettings, setDeviceSettings, getAttributes, getSelfTestLogs, getInformation, getScheduleList, getScheduledTest, setScheduledTest, deleteScheduledTest, executeScheduledTest).

entries.title: File System Management in OMV (Storage > File Systems)
entries.content: File Systems page (Storage > File Systems, /storage/filesystems) manages filesystem creation and mounting. Status codes: 1=Available (detected and mounted), 2=Initializing (being formatted), 3=Missing (configured but not found). Filesystem types supported: ext4, xfs, btrfs, jfs, f2fs. Btrfs creation supports RAID data/metadata profiles: single, dup, RAID0, RAID1, RAID10, RAID5, RAID6. Mount operation: adds entry to OMV config database, creates mount point /srv/UUID/, adds to /etc/fstab via Salt, then mounts. Unmount: removes mount point config, applies fstab changes. Grow: expands filesystem to fill device (ext4 and xfs support online resize). After creating a filesystem, you must mount it before creating Shared Folders on it. OMV mount point paths: /srv/<UUID-of-device>. RPC: FileSystemMgmt (enumerateFilesystems, enumerateMountedFilesystems, getList, getListBg, getCandidates, create, createBtrfs, grow, setMountPoint, umountByFsName, umountByDir, hasFilesystem, getDetails).

entries.title: Shared Folder Management in OMV
entries.content: Shared Folders (Storage > Shared Folders, /storage/shared-folders) define named storage paths that services expose to the network. Prerequisites: filesystem must be mounted. Creating a shared folder: 1) Click Add. 2) Name (globally unique). 3) Select filesystem/volume. 4) Relative path (subdirectory within the volume, cannot contain '..'). 5) Permissions mode (default 775). When created: OMV creates the directory (or btrfs subvolume for btrfs volumes), sets group ownership to 'users', sets setgid bit. Shared folder absolute path: <mount-point>/<relative-path>, e.g. /srv/disk-uuid/myfolder/. Privileges dialog: set per-user and per-group access (no access=NULL, read-only=5, read/write=7). ACL dialog: set POSIX ACL entries for granular per-user/per-group permissions using setfacl/getfacl. Snapshots: available for btrfs-backed shared folders. Delete modes: remove config only (data stays), or remove config AND delete all content (rm -f -r). Cannot delete if referenced by an active service. RPC: ShareMgmt (getCandidates, enumerateSharedFolders, get, set, delete, getPrivileges, setPrivileges, getPrivilegesByRole, setPrivilegesByRole, copyPrivileges, getFileACL, setFileACL, getPath, enumerateSnapshots, createSnapshot, createScheduledSnapshotTask, deleteSnapshot, restoreSnapshot, fromSnapshot, getSnapshotLifecycle, setSnapshotLifecycle).

entries.title: Shared Folder Permissions, Privileges, and ACL
entries.content: OMV uses two permission layers for shared folders. Layer 1 - OMV Privileges (simple): set via Storage > Shared Folders > Privileges button. Values: no access (NULL), read-only (perms=5, maps to r-x), read/write (perms=7, maps to rwx). Applied by OMV Salt state via setfacl/chmod. Layer 2 - POSIX ACL (fine-grained): set via ACL dialog using getfacl/setfacl. Supports named user/group ACL entries, default ACLs (inherited by new files). Requires filesystem to support ACL - ext4, xfs, btrfs do; FAT/NTFS/exFAT do not. Common permission issues and fixes: 1) User cannot access share - check user is in 'users' group (Users > Groups). 2) Correct OMV privilege not working - apply changes via Salt (yellow banner). 3) New files wrong permissions - check setgid bit: ls -la should show 'drwxrwsr-x'. Reset: chmod g+s /srv/UUID/folder. 4) Manual permission reset: chmod -R 775 /srv/UUID/folder && chown -R :users /srv/UUID/folder && chmod g+s /srv/UUID/folder. 5) Admin user cannot be given privileges (web admin only, not a NAS user). 6) After privilege changes, must click Apply in OMV UI and wait for Salt deployment.

entries.title: Software RAID (Multiple Device) in OMV
entries.content: Software RAID is at Storage > Multiple Device (/storage/md). Uses Linux mdadm. RAID levels: RAID 0 (striping, no redundancy), RAID 1 (mirroring, 1 drive can fail, min 2 disks), RAID 4 (dedicated parity disk), RAID 5 (distributed parity, 1 drive can fail, min 3 disks), RAID 6 (double parity, 2 drives can fail, min 4 disks), RAID 10 (striped mirrors, min 4 disks). Workflow: 1) Create RAID device (select level + member disks) -> appears as /dev/mdX. 2) Go to File Systems, create filesystem on /dev/mdX. 3) Mount the filesystem. 4) Create Shared Folders on it. Operations: Grow (add disks to expand array, then resize filesystem), Recover (rebuild degraded array), Remove (stop and delete array). Monitor: cat /proc/mdstat (real-time status). Detail: mdadm --detail /dev/mdX. After reboot, RAID auto-assembles via /etc/mdadm/mdadm.conf. RPC: MdMgmt (enumerateDevices, getList, get, getSlaves, getCandidates, create, grow, add, remove, delete, getDetail).

entries.title: Bcache SSD Caching in OMV
entries.content: Bcache is at Storage > Bcache (/storage/bcache). Allows fast SSDs to cache slow HDDs at the block level. Components: Cache device (SSD) - the fast caching device; Backing device (HDD) - the slow device being cached. Cache modes: writethrough (data written to both SSD cache and HDD simultaneously, safe), writeback (data written to SSD first, then flushed to HDD later, faster but small data loss risk on power failure), writearound (bypass cache for writes, reads still cached). After creation, the backing device appears as /dev/bcacheX and should be used like a normal block device. RPC: bcache (getCacheList, createCache, deleteCache, unregisterCache, getCacheConfiguration, setCacheConfiguration, getCacheStatistic, clearCacheStatistic, getBackingList, getCacheCandidates, createBacking, deleteBacking, getBacking, updateBacking, unregisterBacking, getBackingConfiguration, setBackingConfiguration, forceRunBacking, register, getBackingStatistic, clearBackingStatistic, getSuperBlock).

entries.title: SMB/CIFS (Samba) Configuration in OMV
entries.content: SMB is at Services > SMB/CIFS (/services/smb). Settings: enable/disable Samba globally, workgroup name (default WORKGROUP), server description, enable NetBIOS over TCP (nmbd), enable home directories, enable WINS server support. Shares: create individual Samba shares. Per-share options: name, comment, select shared folder, public/guest access (yes=no auth required), read-only, browseable, enable recycle bin (vfs objects = recycle, with configurable max size and path), inherit owner/permissions, enable ACL support (maps to POSIX ACL), shadow copies. Config file: /etc/samba/smb.conf (managed by OMV Salt). Services: smbd (file sharing daemon), nmbd (NetBIOS name service). After changes: omv-salt deploy run smb. Check config: testparm. View connections: smbstatus. Add user to Samba manually: smbpasswd -a username (OMV does this automatically). Connect from Windows: \\server-ip\sharename. Mount on Linux: mount -t cifs //server/share /mnt -o username=user,password=pass,vers=3.0. RPC: SMB (getSettings, setSettings, getShareList, getShare, setShare, deleteShare, emptyRecycleBin, getStats).

entries.title: NFS Configuration in OMV
entries.content: NFS is at Services > NFS (/services/nfs). Settings: enable/disable NFS server, supported NFS versions (v3, v4). Shares: create NFS exports. Per-share settings: shared folder selection, client (IP address like 192.168.1.100, network like 192.168.1.0/24, or * for all), access type (read/write or read-only), additional options field. File managed: /etc/exports. After changes: omv-salt deploy run nfs, or exportfs -ra. Service: nfs-server. Check exports: exportfs -v. Show exports to client: showmount -e server-ip. Mount from Linux client: mount -t nfs -o vers=4,rw server:/srv/UUID/folder /mnt/target. Key NFS export options: rw (read-write), ro (read-only), sync (safe, write confirmed before ack), async (faster, less safe), no_root_squash (root on client maps to root on server - security risk), root_squash (default, root mapped to nobody), all_squash (all users mapped to anonymous), no_subtree_check (recommended), anonuid/anongid (set anonymous user mapping). Ports: NFS v4 uses 2049 TCP only; NFS v3 uses 2049 TCP/UDP plus portmapper 111. RPC: NFS (getSettings, setSettings, getShareList, getShare, setShare, deleteShare, getStats).

entries.title: SSH Configuration in OMV
entries.content: SSH is at Services > SSH (/services/ssh). Configuration options: enable/disable SSH service, port number (default 22), allow password authentication (disable for key-only access), permit root login (yes/no/forced-commands-only), enable public key authentication, TCP forwarding, compression. SSH keys for individual users: Users > Users > edit user > SSH Public Keys tab. Config file: /etc/ssh/sshd_config (managed by OMV). After changes apply via OMV UI. Check status: systemctl status ssh. Reload config without dropping connections: systemctl reload ssh. RPC: SSH (get, set, getStats).

entries.title: Rsync Configuration in OMV
entries.content: Rsync is at Services > Rsync (/services/rsync). Two components: 1) Rsync Server (rsyncd daemon): Settings sub-page enables the rsync daemon on port 873. Modules sub-page defines named module paths accessible to remote rsync clients. Per-module settings: name, path, comment, auth required, read-only, max connections, allow/deny hosts. Config: /etc/rsyncd.conf. 2) Rsync Tasks (client jobs): Create scheduled sync jobs. Per-task settings: source (local shared folder or remote rsync:// URL), destination, direction (push/pull), schedule (cron-like), recursive, delete extra files, compress, preserve permissions/timestamps. Tasks are saved as cron jobs. Run task immediately: Execute button. RPC: Rsync (getList, get, set, delete, execute) for tasks; Rsyncd (getSettings, setSettings, getModuleList, getModule, setModule, deleteModule) for daemon.

entries.title: Network Interface Configuration in OMV
entries.content: Network configuration is at Network section. General page (/network/general): hostname, domain name, DNS nameservers, IPv4 and IPv6 forwarding enable/disable. Interfaces page (/network/interfaces): lists all detected network interfaces. Interface types supported: Ethernet (physical NIC), Bond (link aggregation, modes: 0=round-robin, 1=active-backup, 4=802.3ad/LACP, etc.), VLAN (802.1Q tagging, parent interface + VLAN ID), Wireless (WiFi, WPA/WPA2), Bridge (software bridge for VMs/containers). Per-interface settings: DHCP or manual IP/mask/gateway/DNS, IPv6 mode, MTU, wake-on-LAN enable. After changes: omv-salt deploy run interfaces. Check: ip addr, ip route, networkctl status. Proxy (/network/proxy): HTTP/HTTPS proxy for apt, system downloads. RPC: Network (getGeneralSettings, setGeneralSettings, enumerateDevices, getInterfaceList, getInterface, deleteInterface, getEthernetIface, setEthernetIface, getBondIface, setBondIface, getVlanIface, setVlanIface, getWirelessIface, setWirelessIface, getBridgeIface, setBridgeIface, getProxy, setProxy, identify, getInformation).

entries.title: Firewall (iptables/ip6tables) in OMV
entries.content: Firewall is at Network > Firewall (/network/firewall/rules). OMV manages iptables (IPv4) and ip6tables (IPv6) rules. Rule parameters: family (inet=IPv4, inet6=IPv6), action (ACCEPT, REJECT, DROP, LOG), chain (INPUT, OUTPUT, FORWARD), protocol (tcp, udp, icmp, all), source address/port, destination address/port. Rules are evaluated top-to-bottom, first match wins. OMV does not add default block rules - it is permissive by default. After changes apply via OMV UI: omv-salt deploy run iptables. View current rules: iptables -L -n -v, ip6tables -L -n -v. Flush all rules (emergency): iptables -F && iptables -X && iptables -P INPUT ACCEPT && iptables -P OUTPUT ACCEPT && iptables -P FORWARD ACCEPT. CRITICAL: always ensure port 80/443 (web UI) and port 22 (SSH) have ACCEPT rules before adding any DROP rules to avoid lockout. RPC: Iptables (getRules, setRules, getRules6, setRules6, getRule, setRule, deleteRule).

entries.title: Email Notifications Setup in OMV
entries.content: Email notifications are at System > Notification (/system/notification). Settings page (SMTP configuration): server address, port (common: 587 for TLS/STARTTLS, 465 for SSL, 25 for unencrypted), TLS/SSL mode (none, STARTTLS, SSL/TLS), authentication (username + password), sender email address, recipient email address. Test Email button sends a verification email. Events page: individual enable/disable per notification category (authentication events, disk health, filesystem usage, RAID events, software updates, service failures). OMV uses Postfix as local MTA configured to relay through the SMTP server. Common SMTP providers: Gmail (smtp.gmail.com:587, STARTTLS, requires App Password if 2FA enabled), Outlook/Hotmail (smtp-mail.outlook.com:587). For Gmail with 2FA: go to Google Account > Security > App Passwords to generate a 16-character app password. RPC: Notification (getList, setList, get, set, isEnabled).

entries.title: Scheduled Tasks (Cron Jobs) in OMV
entries.content: Scheduled Tasks are at System > Scheduled Tasks (/system/cron). Create cron jobs with fields: enable/disable toggle, type (userdefined, reboot, shutdown, standby), execution time (preset: hourly, daily, weekly, monthly, yearly, or custom cron expression), command to run, username to run as (root for system tasks), send email on completion. Cron expression format: 'minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week'. Examples: '0 3 * * 0' = Sundays at 3am, '*/30 * * * *' = every 30 minutes, '0 0 1 * *' = 1st of each month. Jobs are written to /etc/cron.d/ files managed by OMV. Execute immediately: Run button. Common uses: cleanup scripts, custom backups, maintenance tasks. RPC: Cron (getList, get, set, delete, execute).

entries.title: Power Management in OMV
entries.content: Power Management is at System > Power Management (/system/powermgmt). Settings page: configure CPU governor (performance, powersave, ondemand, conservative, userspace). Scheduled Jobs page: create time-based power events (shutdown, reboot, standby/sleep, hibernate). These are implemented as cron jobs. Disk spin-down is configured separately in Storage > Disks via hdparm settings (spindown_time parameter, APM level). For individual disk spin-down: select disk in Storage > Disks, click Edit, configure power management tab. Standby timeout is in units of 5 seconds (value 1-240) or 30 seconds (241-251) for IDE drives. For modern drives, APM level 127 allows spin-down, APM 254 disables APM. RPC: PowerMgmt (get, set, getScheduleList, getScheduledJob, setScheduledJob, deleteScheduledJob, executeScheduledJob, enumerateStandbyModes). System-level commands: poweroff, reboot, systemctl suspend, systemctl hibernate.

entries.title: Certificate and SSH Key Management in OMV
entries.content: Certificates are at System > Certificates (/system/certificate). SSL Certificates (/system/certificate/ssl): Import existing SSL certificate (paste PEM certificate + private key) or generate self-signed certificate (set common name, organization, country, validity period). SSL certificates are used by the OMV web UI for HTTPS (configure in System > Workbench) and by other SSL-enabled services. Generates: .crt and .key files stored in /etc/ssl/. SSH Keys (/system/certificate/ssh): Create SSH key pairs (RSA or ECDSA), import existing public keys, delete keys. The copySshId method copies the public key to a remote server's authorized_keys for passwordless authentication (used by rsync tasks for remote server authentication). After creating SSL cert, go to System > Workbench, select the certificate in the HTTPS settings. RPC: CertificateMgmt (getList, get, set, delete, getDetail, create, getSshList, createSsh, getSsh, setSsh, deleteSsh, copySshId).

entries.title: Plugin Management in OMV
entries.content: Plugins are at System > Plugins (/system/plugins). Shows packages available from configured OMV plugin repositories. Install: click Install button (runs apt-get install). Remove: select installed plugin, click Remove (runs apt-get remove). After plugin install/remove, OMV applies the configuration changes automatically. Popular community plugins (requires omv-extras repository): openmediavault-compose (Docker Compose + Portainer CE), openmediavault-mergerfs (union/pooling filesystem), openmediavault-snapraid (parity-based data protection for large media collections), openmediavault-zfs (ZFS on Linux support), openmediavault-luksencryption (LUKS disk encryption), openmediavault-flashmemory (log2ram, reduces flash wear on SD cards). Plugin packages follow naming: openmediavault-<name>. To list installed plugins: dpkg -l openmediavault-* RPC: Plugin (enumeratePlugins, getList, remove, upload, install).

entries.title: omv-extras Plugin Repository Manager
entries.content: omv-extras (/system/omvextras) is a community-maintained plugin repository manager. Must be installed first before most community plugins are available. After installation, the omv-extras page appears in System > omv-extras. Features: enable/disable omv-extras repository, enable Debian backports repository (provides newer kernel and packages for better hardware support), clean apt cache. After enabling repositories, run Update in System > Update Management to refresh package lists. RPC: omvextras (get, set, backports, clean).

entries.title: Docker and Portainer via omv-extras
entries.content: Docker is not built into OMV core. Available via the omv-extras ecosystem. Steps: 1) Install omv-extras (see omv-extras entry). 2) Go to System > Plugins, search for 'compose' or 'docker'. 3) Install openmediavault-compose plugin. 4) This installs Docker CE and Portainer CE. 5) Access Portainer at http://server-ip:9000 (default, first run setup). Docker data: /var/lib/docker/. Container volumes: use paths from OMV Shared Folders as bind mounts in docker-compose files (e.g., /srv/disk-uuid/mydata:/container/data). After OMV system updates: run omv-salt deploy run systemd to ensure Docker service unit is current. Common Docker commands: docker ps (running containers), docker-compose up -d (start stack), docker-compose down (stop), docker logs <container> (view logs).

entries.title: Applying Configuration Changes in OMV (omv-salt)
entries.content: OMV uses SaltStack to translate database configuration into actual system files. When changes are made in the web UI, a yellow 'Apply' banner appears. Clicking Apply triggers: omv-salt deploy run <changed-modules>. Key command: omv-salt deploy run all (apply all pending changes). Module-specific apply: omv-salt deploy run smb (Samba only), omv-salt deploy run nfs, omv-salt deploy run fstab, omv-salt deploy run interfaces, omv-salt deploy run iptables, omv-salt deploy run monit, omv-salt deploy run cron, omv-salt deploy run postfix, omv-salt deploy run nginx, omv-salt deploy run systemd. After system package upgrades: always run omv-salt deploy run systemd to re-apply systemd service unit files. Config database: /etc/openmediavault/config.xml. Check Salt minion: systemctl status salt-minion. If Salt hangs: systemctl restart salt-minion. OMV engine: systemctl status openmediavault-engined (handles RPC requests from the web UI).

entries.title: Reset OMV Admin Password
entries.content: To reset the OMV web UI admin password when locked out. Method 1 (recommended): Log in via SSH or physical console as root. Run: omv-firstaid. Select the option for 'Reset web administrator password'. Enter and confirm new password. Method 2: If SSH is also unavailable, connect a monitor and keyboard for physical console access. Important distinctions: The OMV web admin password is separate from the Linux root password. The Linux root password is changed with: passwd root (via console). The OMV admin account exists as a system account; OMV web login uses PAM authentication.

entries.title: User and Group Management in OMV
entries.content: User management is at Users section (/usermgmt). Users (/usermgmt/users): create/edit/delete Linux system users. Fields: username (alphanumeric, no spaces), password, shell (default /bin/sh or /usr/sbin/nologin to prevent terminal login), groups, home directory (optional), comment, SSH public keys (for key-based SSH auth), disableaccount toggle. Groups (/usermgmt/groups): create/edit/delete Linux groups, add/remove members. Settings (/usermgmt/settings): default shell, default group for new users (typically 'users'). All users are real Linux accounts added to /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, /etc/group. OMV also adds users to Samba database (smbpasswd) for SMB access. The 'admin' user is the OMV web UI administrator - it cannot receive shared folder privileges and should not be used as a NAS data user. Import users: CSV format (username, password, uid, gid, comment, homedir, shell). RPC: UserMgmt (authUser, enumerateSystemUsers, enumerateUsers, getUserList, getUser, setUser, deleteUser, importUsers, getGroupList, getGroup, setGroup, deleteGroup, importGroups, getSettings, setSettings, setPasswordByContext).

entries.title: System Monitoring and Performance Statistics
entries.content: Monitoring configuration is at System > Monitoring (/system/monitoring). Uses collectd daemon with RRDtool for storing and graphing time-series data. Settings: enable/disable collectd. Performance statistics graphs at Diagnostics > Performance Statistics (/diagnostics/performance-statistics) with sub-pages: CPU (usage per core, system/user/iowait), Memory (RAM usage, swap), System Load (1min/5min/15min averages), Uptime, Network Interfaces (bytes in/out per second per interface), Disk Usage (df - free/used space per mounted filesystem). Data stored in /var/lib/collectd/rrd/. System Information at Diagnostics > System Information shows: CPU model/cores/frequency, total RAM, kernel version, OS version, OMV version, system uptime. System RPC provides: getTopInfo (process list), getCpuStats, getCpuGovernors, getInformation, getDiagnosticReport.

entries.title: ext4 Filesystem: Details, Commands, and Options
entries.content: ext4 (Fourth Extended Filesystem) is the default OMV filesystem choice, most mature and reliable for NAS use. Features: journaling (ordered mode by default - protects metadata, data written before commit), extents (efficient large file allocation), 48-bit block addresses (supports up to 1 EiB volumes), POSIX ACL support, quota support, online grow. Create: mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdXN or mkfs.ext4 -L 'Label' -m 0 /dev/sdXN (m 0 = no reserved blocks). View info: tune2fs -l /dev/sdXN. Filesystem check (offline only): e2fsck -f /dev/sdXN or fsck.ext4 -f /dev/sdXN. Online grow (after expanding block device): resize2fs /dev/sdXN. Set label: tune2fs -L 'NewLabel' /dev/sdXN. Set reserved blocks: tune2fs -m 0 /dev/sdXN (reduce from default 5% to 0 for data drives). Check inode count: df -i /mnt/point. Common mount options: defaults, relatime, noatime (skip access time update - improves SSD life), errors=remount-ro (remount read-only on error). Journal modes (data=): writeback (fastest, metadata journaled only), ordered (default, good balance), journal (safest, all data journaled, slowest). inode: each file needs one inode; if df -i shows 100% but df shows space, too many small files.

entries.title: btrfs Filesystem: Features, Commands, and RAID
entries.content: btrfs (B-tree Filesystem) is a modern copy-on-write filesystem with rich NAS features. OMV 8 has native btrfs support including shared folder snapshots. Key features: Copy-on-Write (CoW) - modifying a file creates new blocks instead of overwriting; Subvolumes - lightweight logical volumes within the filesystem (OMV creates shared folders as btrfs subvolumes on btrfs volumes); Snapshots - instant read-only or read-write copies of subvolumes; Built-in software RAID (0, 1, 10, 5, 6); Transparent compression (zlib, lzo, zstd); Online balance and scrub. Commands: mkfs.btrfs -L 'Label' /dev/sdX (create single), mkfs.btrfs -d raid1 -m raid1 /dev/sda /dev/sdb (multi-device RAID1). Subvolumes: btrfs subvolume create /mnt/subvol, btrfs subvolume list /mnt, btrfs subvolume delete /mnt/subvol. Snapshots: btrfs subvolume snapshot /mnt/subvol /mnt/.snapshots/snap1 (read-write), btrfs subvolume snapshot -r /mnt/subvol /mnt/.snapshots/snap1 (read-only). Scrub (verify checksums, correct errors): btrfs scrub start /mnt, btrfs scrub status /mnt. Balance (redistribute data blocks): btrfs balance start /mnt. Compression mount option: mount -o compress=zstd:1 /dev/sdX /mnt. Check filesystem usage: btrfs filesystem usage /mnt. Known issues: RAID5/6 has known parity bugs in older kernels, use carefully.

entries.title: XFS Filesystem: Features and Commands
entries.content: XFS is a high-performance 64-bit journaling filesystem excellent for large files and high-throughput NAS workloads. Features: journaling (metadata only, very fast recovery), extent-based allocation, online grow only (cannot shrink), quota support (user/group/project), POSIX ACL, delayed allocation. Create: mkfs.xfs /dev/sdXN or mkfs.xfs -L 'Label' /dev/sdXN. View info: xfs_info /mnt/point (must be mounted). Check/repair (offline only): xfs_repair /dev/sdXN. Dry-run check: xfs_repair -n /dev/sdXN. Grow (online, filesystem must be mounted): xfs_growfs /mnt/point. Freeze for consistent snapshot: xfs_freeze -f /mnt/point, xfs_freeze -u /mnt/point (unfreeze). Common mount options: defaults, noatime, logbufs=8 (increase log buffers for performance). XFS cannot shrink - plan partition size carefully. Max file size: 8 EiB. Max volume size: 8 EiB.

entries.title: NTFS, exFAT, tmpfs, and Other Filesystems
entries.content: NTFS (Windows New Technology File System): driver is ntfs-3g on Linux (FUSE-based, slower) or the newer kernel ntfs3 driver. Mount: mount -t ntfs-3g /dev/sdXN /mnt -o uid=1000,gid=1000,umask=022. Or: mount -t ntfs3 /dev/sdXN /mnt. Limitations: no POSIX permissions (use uid/gid/umask mount options), no hard links, no symlinks, slower than native Linux filesystems. Not recommended for NAS data volumes. Good for: external drives shared with Windows, USB drives. exFAT: mount -t exfat /dev/sdXN /mnt. Limitations: no journaling, no POSIX permissions, designed for flash media. Not recommended for NAS data. Good for: SD cards, USB drives, cross-platform compatibility. JFS (IBM Journaled File System): supported by OMV for creation. Mature, low CPU usage, fast journal recovery. F2FS (Flash-Friendly File System): optimized for NAND flash storage (SSDs, eMMC). tmpfs: RAM-based temporary filesystem. Mount: mount -t tmpfs -o size=512M tmpfs /tmp/ramdisk. Size parameter prevents using all RAM (unlike ramfs). Used for /tmp, /run in Linux. Data is lost on reboot. /proc/filesystems: lists kernel-supported filesystem types. Check currently mounted: cat /proc/mounts or mount command.

entries.title: ZFS on Linux (via openmediavault-zfs plugin)
entries.content: ZFS (Zettabyte File System / OpenZFS) is available via the openmediavault-zfs plugin (requires omv-extras). Not a core OMV feature. Concepts: zpool (storage pool containing vdevs), vdev (virtual device: single disk, mirror, RAIDZ1/2/3), dataset (like directory with independent properties), zvol (block device from ZFS), snapshot (read-only point-in-time copy). Pool creation: zpool create tank /dev/sda (single disk), zpool create tank mirror /dev/sda /dev/sdb (mirror), zpool create tank raidz /dev/sda /dev/sdb /dev/sdc (RAIDZ1 = similar to RAID5), zpool create tank raidz2 /dev/sd[abcd] (RAIDZ2 = RAID6). Operations: zpool status (pool health), zpool scrub tank (verify all data checksums), zfs create tank/dataset (new dataset), zfs snapshot tank/dataset@name (snapshot), zfs list (list all), zfs get all tank/dataset (properties). ARC (Adaptive Replacement Cache): in-memory read cache. View: cat /proc/spl/kstat/zfs/arcstats | grep -E 'size|hits|misses'. ZFS needs dedicated RAM; rule of thumb: 1GB RAM per 1TB storage minimum. Compression: zfs set compression=lz4 tank/dataset (recommended, good ratio + performance). Deduplication is very RAM intensive - avoid unless necessary.

entries.title: NFS Exports Syntax and Client Mount Options
entries.content: NFS /etc/exports syntax: /path client(options). Client types: * (all hosts), 192.168.1.100 (single IP), 192.168.1.0/24 (subnet). Export options: rw (read-write), ro (read-only), sync (server confirms write to disk before responding - safe), async (respond before disk write - faster, small data loss risk on crash), no_root_squash (root on client = root on server - security risk), root_squash (default - client root mapped to nfsnobody/65534), all_squash (all client users mapped to anonymous uid/gid), anonuid=1000 (set anonymous UID), anongid=1000 (set anonymous GID), no_subtree_check (recommended - avoids issues when files are renamed while open). After editing /etc/exports: exportfs -ra (reload without restart), exportfs -v (verbose list), systemctl restart nfs-server (full restart). NFSv4 uses a virtual root; all exports are relative to the NFSv4 root (usually /). Client mount: mount -t nfs4 server:/path /mnt (NFSv4), mount -t nfs -o vers=3 server:/path /mnt (NFSv3). Common client options: hard (retry forever on server unreachable), soft (timeout and return error), timeo=600 (timeout in deciseconds).

entries.title: SMB/CIFS Share Configuration and Client Mount
entries.content: Samba smb.conf per-share config: [sharename], path = /srv/uuid/folder, comment = My Share, valid users = @users (all in 'users' group) or user1 user2, write list = @users, read only = no, create mask = 0664, directory mask = 2775 (setgid bit), guest ok = no. Recycle bin: vfs objects = recycle, recycle:repository = .recycle, recycle:maxsize = 0. Shadow copies (btrfs): vfs objects = shadow_copy2, shadow:snapdir = .snapshots. Test config: testparm (check smb.conf syntax). Check connections: smbstatus. List shares: smbclient -L //server -U user. Connect: smbclient //server/share -U user. Mount CIFS on Linux: mount -t cifs //server/share /mnt -o username=user,password=pass,vers=3.0,uid=1000,gid=1000. Using credentials file: mount -t cifs //server/share /mnt -o credentials=/etc/.cifs-creds,vers=3.0. /etc/.cifs-creds contents: username=myuser, password=mypass, domain=WORKGROUP. fstab entry: //server/share /mnt cifs credentials=/etc/.cifs-creds,vers=3.0,uid=1000,gid=1000,iocharset=utf8 0 0.

entries.title: /proc and /sys Key Files for System Monitoring
entries.content: /proc key monitoring files: /proc/meminfo - RAM stats (MemTotal, MemFree, MemAvailable, Buffers, Cached, SwapTotal, SwapFree, Dirty, Writeback); /proc/cpuinfo - CPU model name, cpu MHz, cache size, flags; /proc/diskstats - disk I/O stats (reads completed, sectors read, writes completed, sectors written, I/Os in progress, ms total); /proc/mounts - currently mounted filesystems (device, mountpoint, fstype, options); /proc/mdstat - software RAID status (array state, rebuild progress, sync speed); /proc/net/dev - network interface statistics (bytes, packets, errors, drops per interface); /proc/loadavg - system load (1min 5min 15min running/total lastpid); /proc/uptime - seconds since boot, seconds CPU idle; /proc/partitions - block device partitions. /sys key paths: /sys/block/sdX/queue/scheduler - I/O scheduler (read current, echo 'mq-deadline' > scheduler to change); /sys/block/sdX/queue/rotational - 0=SSD, 1=HDD; /sys/block/sdX/size - size in 512-byte sectors; /sys/class/scsi_host/hostX/scan - write '- - -' to rescan SCSI; /sys/class/net/ethX/statistics/ - network stats; /sys/class/hwmon/hwmonX/temp1_input - temperature in millidegrees.

entries.title: Disk Not Showing Up in OMV
entries.content: Troubleshooting a physical disk that does not appear in Storage > Disks: 1) Click Rescan SCSI Bus button in the Disks page. 2) Check OS detection: lsblk -f (list block devices with filesystem info), ls /dev/sd* (list SATA/SAS devices), ls /dev/nvme* (NVMe drives). 3) Check dmesg for drive events: dmesg | grep -i 'sd\|sata\|ata\|disk\|block' | tail -30. 4) USB drives: lsusb, dmesg | tail -20 after plugging in. 5) Drive with existing filesystem: blkid shows filesystem but OMV may not show as mountable if already configured in another mount point. Check cat /etc/fstab. 6) Drives already in use by OMV (has a configured mount point) are shown but may be marked in-use. 7) Root OS disk is shown but marked read-only. 8) Hardware RAID controller: controller may present only logical volumes, not physical disks. 9) Check /proc/partitions for all block devices. 10) For hotplug SATA: check SATA hot-plug support in BIOS/UEFI. 11) If NVMe: check if nvme driver loaded: lsmod | grep nvme.

entries.title: Network Share Not Accessible
entries.content: Share not accessible from network clients. SMB/Windows troubleshooting: 1) Verify SMB enabled in Services > SMB > Settings. 2) Check Samba services: systemctl status smbd nmbd. 3) Verify share exists in Services > SMB > Shares with correct shared folder. 4) Check user privileges on shared folder in Storage > Shared Folders > Privileges. 5) Ensure user is in 'users' group: Users > Groups. 6) Check firewall ports: 445 (TCP/SMB), 139 (TCP/NetBIOS), 137-138 (UDP/NetBIOS). 7) Test from command line: smbclient -L //server-ip -U username. 8) Windows credential cache: Control Panel > Credential Manager > clear saved Windows Credentials. 9) Check testparm for config errors. 10) For guest access, verify 'public = yes' in share settings. NFS troubleshooting: 1) Verify NFS enabled: Services > NFS > Settings. 2) Service check: systemctl status nfs-server. 3) List current exports: exportfs -v. 4) Test from server: showmount -e localhost. 5) Check firewall: port 2049 (TCP/UDP) and 111 (portmapper for NFSv3). 6) NFSv4 only needs port 2049. 7) Check client mount options match server (vers=4 or vers=3). 8) Verify client IP matches export client specification.

entries.title: Permission Denied on Shared Folder Access
entries.content: Users getting 'Permission Denied', 'Access Denied', or 'NT_STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED': 1) Check OMV privileges: Storage > Shared Folders > select folder > Privileges button. Set user to read/write (7) or read-only (5). Apply changes. 2) Check group membership: Users > Groups, edit 'users' group, ensure the user is a member. 3) Verify filesystem ACL: ls -la /srv/UUID/ should show group 'users' with write permissions. Directory should have 'drwxrwsr-x' (note the 's' = setgid). 4) For SMB: verify the user exists in Samba: pdbedit -L. 5) Check if filesystem supports ACL: ext4, xfs, btrfs = yes; FAT/NTFS/exFAT = no. 6) If ACL set manually and conflicting, reset: setfacl -b /srv/UUID/folder (remove all ACL). 7) Check if Salt applied successfully after privilege change. 8) Manual permission fix: chmod -R 775 /srv/UUID/folder && chown -R :users /srv/UUID/folder && chmod g+s /srv/UUID/folder. 9) For NFS: check export options (root_squash/no_root_squash, all_squash). 10) Ensure the shared folder path exists: ls -la /srv/UUID/foldername.

entries.title: OMV Web UI Not Loading or Unreachable
entries.content: Web UI not accessible at http://server-ip or https://server-ip: 1) Check nginx: systemctl status nginx. If failed: systemctl restart nginx. Check nginx errors: journalctl -u nginx -n 50 or tail /var/log/nginx/error.log. 2) Check PHP-FPM: systemctl status php*-fpm. Restart: systemctl restart php8.2-fpm (version may differ). 3) Check OMV engine (API backend): systemctl status openmediavault-engined. Restart: systemctl restart openmediavault-engined. 4) Check listening ports: ss -tlnp | grep -E '80|443'. 5) Check if IP address changed: ip addr show. Ping server, try new IP. 6) Firewall might block port 80/443: iptables -L -n | grep -E '80|443'. 7) If SSL misconfigured, try HTTP: http://server-ip. 8) Reapply nginx config: omv-salt deploy run nginx. 9) If nginx config broken: nginx -t (check syntax). 10) Last resort: reboot server (if physical access available). 11) After reboot, check: journalctl -xe | head -50.

entries.title: Plugin Installation Failures
entries.content: Plugin installation fails or errors occur: 1) Refresh package lists: System > Update Management > click Check. 2) Ensure required repositories are enabled: if plugin needs omv-extras, install it first. 3) Check disk space: df -h / (root filesystem needs free space). Minimum 1-2GB free. 4) Check internet: ping -c 3 8.8.8.8, apt-get update (from SSH). 5) Manual install: apt-get install openmediavault-<pluginname>. 6) If apt locked: rm -f /var/lib/dpkg/lock-frontend /var/lib/dpkg/lock /var/lib/apt/lists/lock && dpkg --configure -a. 7) After any package install/upgrade: omv-salt deploy run all. 8) After package upgrade causing issues: omv-salt deploy run systemd. 9) Check apt history: tail -50 /var/log/apt/history.log. 10) If dependency conflicts: apt-get -f install (fix broken packages). 11) After removing a plugin, run omv-salt deploy run all to clean up its config.

entries.title: After Package Upgrade: Services Not Starting or Misbehaving
entries.content: After running system updates (Update Management or apt upgrade on CLI), services may not behave correctly. The essential fix command is: omv-salt deploy run systemd (re-generates and applies systemd service unit files). Full apply: omv-salt deploy run all. If salt-minion itself is broken after upgrade: apt-get install --reinstall salt-minion, then systemctl restart salt-minion && omv-salt deploy run all. Check what is failing: journalctl -xe | head -100 (recent errors), systemctl --failed (list failed units). Common post-upgrade issues: nginx fails (run omv-salt deploy run nginx), PHP version mismatch (run omv-salt deploy run nginx), Samba version change (run omv-salt deploy run smb), NFS kernel module changes (run omv-salt deploy run nfs && systemctl restart nfs-server). Always use OMV's Update Management page for upgrades rather than apt directly to avoid issues. If the OMV web UI becomes inaccessible after upgrade, SSH in and run: omv-salt deploy run all.

entries.title: WARNING: Disk Wipe - Irreversible Data Loss
entries.content: CRITICAL WARNING - DATA LOSS. Wiping a disk PERMANENTLY destroys ALL data and partition tables. This cannot be undone. Before suggesting any disk wipe operation: 1) Explicitly warn the user that ALL DATA on the disk will be permanently destroyed. 2) Require user to confirm they have backups of any important data. 3) Confirm the correct device is targeted - double-check with lsblk or fdisk -l. Mistaking /dev/sda for /dev/sdb destroys the wrong disk. 4) Never suggest wiping the system/OS disk (usually /dev/sda or the disk OMV is installed on). 5) The OMV Wipe function uses: sgdisk --zap-all /dev/sdX (destroy partition table) + dd if=/dev/zero of=/dev/sdX bs=10M count=1 (zero first 10MiB) + dd to zero last 10MiB. Secure wipe uses shred -v -n 1. Commands equally dangerous (DO NOT suggest without clear warnings): dd if=/dev/zero of=/dev/sdX, dd if=/dev/urandom of=/dev/sdX, shred /dev/sdX, sgdisk --zap-all /dev/sdX, parted /dev/sdX mklabel gpt. Always trigger the safety warning for these.

entries.title: WARNING: Network Configuration Changes Risk Lockout
entries.content: CAUTION - LOCKOUT RISK. Changing network interface configuration (IP address, subnet mask, gateway, DNS, interface type) can make the OMV server unreachable via network. Steps to minimize risk: 1) Warn user that they may lose network access temporarily or permanently if settings are wrong. 2) Recommend having physical (keyboard+monitor) or out-of-band access available before making changes. 3) Verify the new static IP is in the correct subnet and the gateway is correct and reachable. 4) After applying, the server may be briefly unreachable during network restart. 5) Recovery if locked out: physical console, run 'ip addr add <IP>/<mask> dev <interface> && ip route add default via <gateway>' to restore temporary connectivity, then fix OMV config. Or: omv-firstaid (option to configure network). 6) Changing from DHCP to static: note the current IP assignment before switching.

entries.title: WARNING: Restarting Services Causes Disruption
entries.content: CAUTION. Restarting system services disrupts active users and connections. Services and their impact: nginx restart - web UI becomes unavailable for 1-5 seconds; smbd/nmbd restart - active SMB file transfers drop, Windows clients may show 'network path not available'; nfs-server restart - NFS mounts may hang or become unresponsive on clients (requires remount on client side); sshd restart - existing SSH sessions may disconnect (use 'systemctl reload ssh' instead to reload config without killing sessions); openmediavault-engined restart - web UI API unavailable for seconds. Best practices: 1) Use 'reload' instead of 'restart' when supported (systemctl reload smbd, systemctl reload ssh). 2) Restart during low-usage periods. 3) After restart, verify: systemctl status <service>.

entries.title: WARNING: Modifying /etc/fstab Can Break Boot
entries.content: CAUTION - BOOT FAILURE RISK. Incorrect /etc/fstab entries can prevent the system from booting. OMV manages /etc/fstab automatically via Salt (do NOT edit manually). If editing /etc/fstab is absolutely necessary: 1) Always backup first: cp /etc/fstab /etc/fstab.backup. 2) Use UUID= identifiers instead of /dev/sdX (device names can change after reboots). Get UUID: blkid /dev/sdXN. 3) After editing, test without rebooting: mount -a (mounts all unmounted fstab entries) and check for errors. 4) Use findmnt --verify to check fstab syntax. 5) The 'nofail' option prevents boot failure if the device is not present. 6) If system fails to boot due to bad fstab: boot with init=/bin/bash via GRUB, mount -o remount,rw /, edit /etc/fstab. Or use rescue/live media.

entries.title: WARNING: Changing Passwords
entries.content: CAUTION. Password changes have important implications: 1) OMV web UI admin password: changed in OMV settings or via omv-firstaid. Separate from Linux root password. If forgotten: omv-firstaid > reset web administrator password. 2) Linux root password: change with 'passwd root' from console. If lost: boot into rescue mode via GRUB (add 'init=/bin/bash' to kernel parameters), then 'mount -o remount,rw / && passwd root'. 3) NAS user password changed via OMV UI: updates both Linux /etc/shadow AND Samba database (smbpasswd) automatically. 4) If changing password via 'passwd username' CLI: Samba password is NOT automatically updated. Run: smbpasswd username (to sync). 5) Do not change passwords of system accounts: www-data, openmediavault, nobody, salt - this can break OMV services. 6) SSH key-based auth: changing password does not affect SSH key authentication.

entries.title: WARNING: Firewall Rules Can Lock You Out
entries.content: CRITICAL CAUTION - LOCKOUT RISK. Incorrect iptables firewall rules can block access to OMV's web UI or SSH, requiring physical console access to recover. Before adding any DROP or REJECT rules: 1) Ensure an ACCEPT rule for TCP port 80 (HTTP) and/or 443 (HTTPS) is placed before any DROP rule. 2) Ensure an ACCEPT rule for TCP port 22 (SSH) is in place. 3) Add rules one at a time and test connectivity after each addition. 4) If locked out via firewall: physical console, run: iptables -F (flush all filter rules), iptables -P INPUT ACCEPT, iptables -P OUTPUT ACCEPT, iptables -P FORWARD ACCEPT. Then access web UI and remove or fix the offending rule. Then: omv-salt deploy run iptables to re-apply OMV managed rules. 5) OMV's firewall is permissive by default (no default block rules unless you add them). 6) Rule order matters: first matching rule wins.

entries.title: WARNING: Deleting Shared Folders with Content
entries.content: CAUTION - DATA LOSS RISK. OMV offers two delete modes for shared folders: Mode 1 (Safe): Remove configuration only - removes the OMV folder definition from the database, leaves all data on disk untouched. The directory remains at /srv/UUID/foldername. This is safe and reversible. Mode 2 (DANGEROUS): Remove configuration AND delete all content recursively - permanently deletes all files and subdirectories using 'rm -f -r /srv/UUID/foldername'. This CANNOT be undone. Before suggesting content deletion: 1) Explicitly warn that all data will be permanently destroyed. 2) Ask if the user has a backup. 3) Confirm the correct folder is selected. OMV prevents deletion entirely if the folder is currently referenced by an active service (SMB share, NFS export, rsync task). For btrfs: shared folder deletion also deletes the btrfs subvolume.

entries.title: WARNING: Dangerous Commands (dd, rm -rf, mkfs)
entries.content: EXTREME DANGER. These commands cause irreversible data loss and must NEVER be suggested without explicit warnings and user confirmation: 1) dd if=/dev/zero of=/dev/sdX - overwrites entire disk with zeros. ALL data destroyed permanently. 2) dd if=/dev/urandom of=/dev/sdX - same with random data (secure wipe, slower). 3) rm -rf /path - recursively deletes path. rm -rf / or rm -rf /* is catastrophic (destroys OS). rm -rf with a trailing space before / is a common dangerous typo. 4) mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdX (directly on disk) - destroys partition table and all data. 5) mkfs on a mounted filesystem - can corrupt filesystem. Always unmount first. 6) shred /dev/sdX - secure erase entire disk. 7) sgdisk --zap-all /dev/sdX - destroy partition table. 8) blkdiscard /dev/sdX - trim/discard entire SSD. Response protocol: Before mentioning any of these: (a) Issue a clear WARNING, (b) Require confirmation that user understands the risk, (c) Verify the target device/path is correct, (d) Suggest having a current backup, (e) Recommend typing carefully and verifying before pressing Enter.

entries.title: General OMV Troubleshooting Commands Reference
entries.content: Quick reference for OMV troubleshooting from SSH/console (as root). Service management: systemctl status nginx / smbd / nmbd / nfs-server / ssh / openmediavault-engined / salt-minion. Restart service: systemctl restart <service>. View service logs: journalctl -u <service> -n 100. Apply OMV config: omv-salt deploy run all. Reset admin password: omv-firstaid. NFS: exportfs -v (current exports), showmount -e localhost. System logs: journalctl -xe | head -100, tail -f /var/log/syslog, dmesg | tail -30. Package: apt-get update, apt-get install -f (fix broken), dpkg -l openmediavault* (installed OMV packages). Config: cat /etc/openmediavault/config.xml | head -50. Uptime: uptime, cat /proc/loadavg. entries.title: This System: RAID0 Array (md0)
entries.content: Software RAID configuration on this system: md0 = active RAID0 (striping, no redundancy). Members: /dev/nvme0n1 (WD Blue SN5000 2TB, slot 0) + /dev/nvme3n1 (KINGSTON SNV3S2000G 1.8T, slot 1). Total capacity: 3,906,764,800 blocks (3.6TB), 512k chunk size, super 1.2. Status check: cat /proc/mdstat. Detail: sudo mdadm --detail /dev/md0. IMPORTANT: RAID0 has NO redundancy — if either nvme0n1 or nvme3n1 fails, ALL data is lost. No automatic rebuild possible. Backup is critical. The nvme1n1 (WD_BLACK SN850X) serves as bcache cache layer on top of md0, NOT as a RAID redundancy device. To check bcache status: cat /sys/block/bcache0/bcache/state. bcache modes: writeback (default, fast but data loss on power cut without flush), writethrough (safe, slower), none (cache disabled).

entries.title: This System: bcache Cache Layer
entries.content: bcache (Block Cache) is active on this system. /dev/nvme1n1 (WD_BLACK SN850X 2000GB — fast NVMe) caches reads/writes to /dev/md0 (WD Blue + Kingston RAID0 — slower NVMe). bcache device: /dev/bcache0. Check cache status: cat /sys/block/bcache0/bcache/state (should be 'clean'). Check stats: ls /sys/block/bcache0/bcache/stats_total/. Cache modes: writeback (data written to cache first, flushed to backing device later — faster but risk of data loss on sudden power cut), writethrough (written to both simultaneously — safe), none (bypass cache). Check current mode: cat /sys/block/bcache0/bcache/cache_mode. Change mode: echo writeback > /sys/block/bcache0/bcache/cache_mode. Cache hit rate: cat /sys/block/bcache0/bcache/stats_total/cache_hit_ratio. Bcache is managed at the kernel block layer — OMV's file system management sees bcache0 as a regular block device.

entries.title: OMV Agent v1.4.0: What the Agent Can Answer and How
entries.content:
The OMV Agent Helper (v1.4.0) is a live, daemon-backed assistant embedded in every OMV 8 page. It does NOT use a cloud AI — all intelligence comes from four background daemons reading system state continuously.

WHAT THE AGENT CAN ANSWER WITH LIVE DATA (refreshed every 5-30 seconds):
- CPU temperature: reads /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp every 5s. Ask: 'cpu temp', 'how hot is the processor'
- NVMe drive temperatures: all four drives via nvme-cli and smartctl every 30s
- RAID array status: /proc/mdstat + mdadm --detail for every md device
- bcache status: writeback_running, dirty_data, cache_mode, writeback_percent from sysfs
- Service status: openmediavault-pwmfan, freenove-case-pro, nginx, smbd, docker, jellyfin, and 20+ more
- Filesystem: mounted filesystems filtered (no Docker overlay noise), block device tree
- System load, memory, uptime
- Pending apt updates
- Anomaly detection: high temps, degraded RAID, failed services, full disks

RESPONSE FORMAT (v1.4.0):
Every answer is structured as: direct answer with status icons (✅ ❌ ⏸ ⚠️) at the top, followed by a Tips section with actionable recommendations. No markdown — clean plain text with unicode dividers.

WHAT THE AGENT CANNOT DO:
- Cannot execute commands on your behalf
- Cannot modify OMV configuration
- Cannot access the internet
- All suggestions require your explicit action

entries.title: OMV Agent: Four-Daemon Architecture and How It Works
entries.content:
The OMV Agent runs four independent systemd daemons. Each is isolated with its own system user and minimal privileges.

1. omv-agent.service (user: www-data)
   Flask API on 127.0.0.1:11111. Handles chat queries. Reads the probe cache and knowledge base.    Proxied through OMV's existing nginx — never directly reachable from LAN.

2. omv-agent-probe.service (user: root — required for hardware access)
   Reads hardware state every 5 seconds (load, memory, network, disk, services, CPU temp)    and every 30 seconds (NVMe temps, RAID, bcache, ZFS, apt updates).    Writes structured JSON to /run/omv-agent/probe_cache.json.    From v1.3.0: load averages read from collectd RRD at /var/lib/rrdcached/db/localhost/load/load.rrd —    avoids duplicating collectd's existing metric collection.

3. omv-agent-watch.service (user: omv-agent-watch, PrivateNetwork=yes)
   Tails systemd journal for errors, watches udev for block device changes,    diffs service states. When something goes wrong, writes to the event queue    and the assistant badge lights up. Cannot reach the network at the kernel level.

4. omv-agent-discover.service (user: omv-agent-watch, PrivateNetwork=yes)
   Polls /var/lib/dpkg/info/, /etc/systemd/system/, /etc/nginx/openmediavault-webgui.d/,    /etc/cron.d/, /etc/apt/sources.list.d/ every 10 seconds.    When new packages, services, or configs are added, fires an alert: what arrived, where it is, what to do next.

DATA FLOW: daemons → /run/omv-agent/ → Flask API → nginx proxy → browser widget
No data ever leaves the NAS. No external API calls. Fully air-gapped.

entries.title: OMV Agent: Event Queue, Badge Alerts, and Plugin API
entries.content:
The OMV Agent has a proactive alert system — it notifies you of problems before you ask.

EVENT QUEUE: /run/omv-agent/event_queue.json
Ring buffer of up to 100 events. Each event has: id, timestamp, level (info/warning/critical), type, source, and message. Written atomically by the watcher and discoverer daemons.

FAB BADGE: The floating assistant button shows a red badge with a count when unread events exist. The widget polls /omv-agent/events every 20 seconds. Opening the panel clears the badge.

ALERT TRIGGERS:
- Service fails or enters failed state
- Block device disappears from the system (drive dropped)
- RAID array degrades
- Drive temperature exceeds warning threshold
- Disk usage exceeds 85% (warning) or 95% (critical)
- New package installed (dpkg)
- New systemd service registered
- New apt repository added (warning — verify the source)

PLUGIN-WIDE API (aligned with votdev recommendation):
Any other OMV plugin can push events to the assistant badge via:
POST /omv-agent/events (localhost only)
Body: {level, type, source, msg}
This makes the omv-agent event system shared infrastructure — other plugins can surface their own alerts through the assistant without needing their own notification system.

entries.title: OMV Agent: Version History and What Changed in v1.6.0
entries.content:
Version history and key improvements per release:

v1.0.0 — Initial release
Basic knowledge base assistant with 55 general OMV entries. Static answers only.

v1.1.0 — Live system probes
Added omv-agent-probe.service daemon. Live NVMe temps, RAID status, bcache writeback, service health, disk usage, system load. Added omv-agent-watch.service for journal tailing and udev monitoring.

v1.2.0 — Watcher daemon + event queue
Full watcher daemon with service state diffing, device monitoring, anomaly detection. FAB badge alerts. POST /events endpoint.

v1.3.0 — votdev alignment: RRD integration + plugin API + discovery daemon
Load averages now read from collectd's existing RRD data (no metric duplication). POST /omv-agent/events open API so any plugin can push alerts. New omv-agent-discover.service daemon watching for new packages, services, configs.

v1.4.0 — Detailed answers, clean formatting, two PWM services, CPU temp live probe
All responses restructured: direct answer + Tips section with actionable recommendations. CPU temperature now a live probe from thermal_zone0 (not a static KB answer). Services response parsed into clean bullet lines with ✅ ❌ ⏸ status icons. df output filtered — Docker overlays, tmpfs, udev removed. Both openmediavault-pwmfan and freenove-case-pro independently queryable. 34 markdown instances removed — all responses safe for textContent rendering. Alias map extended: pwmfan, omv-pwmfan, openmediavault-pwmfan all resolve correctly.

v1.5.1 — Version alignment and packaging refresh
Package metadata, backend health endpoint, capabilities response, Workbench display strings, repository index metadata, and bundled knowledge metadata are aligned on 1.5.1.

v1.6.0 — Local Ollama fallback for human phrasing
When the deterministic relevance gate or knowledge base cannot understand a natural-language OMV/NAS/Linux question, the backend can ask a local loopback-only Ollama/Qwen model to rewrite or answer it. Live probes remain authoritative for system data, the backend still cannot execute commands, and systemd network policy limits omv-agent traffic to localhost.
